newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss money tightness may stem from bank action.
newsitem.headline: Swiss money tightness may stem from bank action.

text.p: Swiss money market rates have been tight for the last week and some dealers believe one bank is witholding liquidity.
"For the past week, one large bank has been withholding liquidity from the market," said one money market trader who asked not to be named, echoing reports from other banks.
Traders on Friday morning quoted tomorrow/next money at 1-7/8 to 2.00 percent, against levels at the end of last month around 1.50 percent.

They said the Swiss National Bank (SNB) added liquidity to the market on an overnight basis on Thursday morning, and was said to have offered funds to at least one large bank later in the afternoon on Thursday. It was not seen adding on Friday.

The Swiss money market is considered quite small, consisting largely of three big banks, and therefore is easy to manipulate, traders said. Such activity is not illegal but the central bank frowns on it.
The SNB also does not make public the rates set on its money market operations, its main tool for steering liquidity.

Traders do not believe the tightness stems from any SNB move, citing high level of sight deposits, and statements on Thursday by the SNB's chief economist Georg Rich, who said the SNB had provided funds to the market to counter tightness.

Instead, many believe one bank is withholding funds from the money market in an effort to drive short-term rates higher before expiration of the Swiss three-month interest rate contract on LIFFE on March 17.
A trader at a second bank said that with such a strategy, a bank would lose some returns from the money market, because it would not earn interest on the funds it does not lend out.
But at the same time it could make a handsome profit if it held large short positions in the three-month futures contract, providing the price of the futures contract falls.
"We were a bit surprised to see the Euroswiss move tick for tick in line with the money market rates," said one EuroSwiss dealer based in London.
"The price action certainly has been strange. It has certainly been under more pressure than I would expect," he said, adding such price behaviour could reflect aggressive short selling.
The March contract had fallen sharply to a recent low of 98.04 on Wednesday from a recent high of 98.37 on March 4.
It was up again at 98.12 on Friday.
Banks active in the market are also perplexed by the recent tightness given a relatively high level of sight deposits.
Sight deposits are non-interest bearing accounts the National Bank keeps for banks, public authorities, foreign central banks and commercial banks, and international organisations.
The deposits, reported every 10 days, stood at roughly 3.55 billion Swiss francs at the end of the reporting period on March 10.
